data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Cutaneous tuberculosis** (Leprosy & mycobacterial)_

**Q1. What is cutaneous tuberculosis? How common is it?**
- Infection of skin by M. tuberculosis (rarely M. bovis, BCG) — about 0.1–1% of dermatology patients in India; ~1–2% of extrapulmonary TB
- Commonest Indian forms: lupus vulgaris (adults) and scrofuloderma (children)

**Q2. Classify cutaneous TB (asked very often).**
- True (bacilli in skin): primary — tuberculous chancre (inoculation in a non-immune person); secondary (prior immunity) — lupus vulgaris (haematogenous/lymphatic or exogenous), tuberculosis verrucosa cutis (exogenous re-inoculation), scrofuloderma (contiguous spread), orificial TB (autoinoculation), tuberculous gumma/metastatic abscess (haematogenous), acute miliary TB
- Tuberculids (no bacilli; hypersensitivity): lichen scrofulosorum, papulonecrotic tuberculid, erythema induratum of Bazin (nodular), ± erythema nodosum/nodular tuberculid
- Also classified by bacillary load: multibacillary (chancre, scrofuloderma, orificial, miliary, gumma) vs paucibacillary (LV, TBVC)

**Q3. How does host immunity decide the clinical form?**
- High immunity: TBVC, LV, tuberculids (few bacilli, strong tuberculin)
- Low immunity: miliary, orificial, gumma in malnourished/immunosuppressed; scrofuloderma intermediate
- Th1/Th17 polarisation → localised disease; Th2/Treg → disseminated

**Q4. Describe lupus vulgaris.**
- Chronic progressive paucibacillary form in previously sensitised person; in India mostly on buttocks, trunk, limbs (face in the West)
- Soft reddish-brown plaques that spread at one edge and scar at the other; apple-jelly nodules on diascopy
- Types: plaque (commonest), ulcerative, vegetating, hypertrophic/tumid, papulonodular, sporotrichoid
- Complications: scarring, contractures, mutilation (nose, ear), squamous cell carcinoma in old scars (lupus carcinoma)

**Q5. What is diascopy and its significance?**
- Pressing a glass slide on the lesion blanches erythema to show the yellow-brown 'apple-jelly' colour of granulomas
- Seen in lupus vulgaris, sarcoidosis, granulomatous rosacea, lupus miliaris disseminatus faciei, leishmaniasis, tuberculoid leprosy

**Q6. Describe tuberculosis verrucosa cutis (TBVC).**
- Exogenous re-infection in an immune host — 'prosector's wart', 'butcher's wart'; on hands, knees, ankles, buttocks of barefoot walkers and those who sit on the ground
- Warty plaque with irregular edge, fissures that may ooze pus on pressure; slow peripheral spread, central healing with atrophic scar
- Histology: pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, hyperkeratosis, abscesses in upper dermis, tuberculoid granulomas deeper

**Q7. Describe scrofuloderma.**
- Direct extension from an underlying tuberculous focus — cervical lymph node (commonest), bone, joint, epididymis
- Firm painless subcutaneous swelling → cold abscess → breaks to form undermined ulcers and sinuses discharging cheesy material; bridged (cord-like) scars
- Children and young adults; tuberculin strongly positive; bacilli may be found in pus

**Q8. Differential diagnosis of scrofuloderma.**
- Atypical mycobacterial lymphadenitis, actinomycosis (sulphur granules), mycetoma, sporotrichosis, hidradenitis suppurativa (axilla/groin), lymphogranuloma venereum (inguinal), syphilitic gumma, deep fungal infection, pyogenic abscess, branchial cyst sinus

**Q9. Differential diagnosis of lupus vulgaris.**
- Tuberculoid leprosy (anaesthesia, nerve), sarcoidosis, discoid lupus (follicular plugs, atrophy), chromoblastomycosis, leishmaniasis, psoriasis (plaque LV), tertiary syphilis (serpiginous, gumma), deep fungal infection, Bowen's disease, granuloma annulare, tinea (KOH)

**Q10. What is tuberculous chancre?**
- Primary inoculation in a non-immune person (child) after trauma — injection, circumcision, ear piercing, tattooing
- Painless papulonodule → firm shallow ulcer with granular base after 2–3 weeks + marked regional lymphadenopathy (tuberculous primary complex of skin)
- Tuberculin negative at first, converts later; bacilli plentiful; differential: sporotrichosis, cat-scratch disease, primary syphilis, atypical mycobacteria

**Q11. What is orificial tuberculosis?**
- Painful shallow ulcers at mouth, anus, genitals — autoinoculation from advanced internal TB (lung, intestine, urinary) in a poorly immune host; bacilli many; poor prognosis

**Q12. What is a tuberculous gumma (metastatic tuberculous abscess)?**
- Haematogenous spread in immunosuppressed/malnourished children → firm subcutaneous nodules on trunk/limbs which break down into ulcers and sinuses

**Q13. Define tuberculids and list the criteria.**
- Skin eruptions associated with TB elsewhere, thought to be hypersensitivity to bacilli or antigens
- Criteria: typical clinical and histological picture; no bacilli by stain/culture (PCR may be positive); strongly positive Mantoux/IGRA; evidence of present or past TB; response to ATT

**Q14. Describe lichen scrofulosorum.**
- Grouped asymptomatic tiny follicular/perifollicular yellow-brown lichenoid papules on the trunk of children/young adults, often with tuberculous lymph nodes or bone
- Histology: superficial non-caseating granulomas around follicles and sweat ducts
- Differential: lichen nitidus, keratosis pilaris, lichenoid sarcoid, frictional lichenoid eruption

**Q15. Describe papulonecrotic tuberculid.**
- Symmetrical crops of dusky red papules with central necrosis/crust on extensor limbs, knees, elbows, ears, buttocks; heal with varioliform scars
- Histology: wedge-shaped dermal necrosis with vasculitis (leukocytoclastic or granulomatous)
- Differential: PLEVA, lymphomatoid papulosis, perforating disorders, secondary syphilis, prurigo

**Q16. Describe erythema induratum of Bazin.**
- Recurrent tender deep nodules on the backs of calves of young/middle-aged women; may ulcerate and scar
- Lobular panniculitis with vasculitis, caseation and granulomas
- Nodular vasculitis = non-TB counterpart; differential: erythema nodosum (shins, no ulceration, septal panniculitis), polyarteritis nodosa

**Q17. How will you investigate cutaneous TB?**
- Histopathology (tuberculoid granulomas ± caseation) and tissue culture — ideally two biopsies: one for HPE, one for culture/CBNAAT
- Ziehl–Neelsen stain (low yield in paucibacillary forms); culture — LJ medium (4–8 weeks) or liquid MGIT (faster, more sensitive), with drug-susceptibility testing
- CBNAAT/GeneXpert MTB/RIF (rifampicin resistance in ~2 h) and TrueNat — recommended by NTEP; PCR (IS6110) helpful in paucibacillary forms
- Mantoux test (strongly positive in LV, TBVC, tuberculids) and IGRA (QuantiFERON) — support, not diagnose
- Look for systemic focus: chest X-ray, ultrasound abdomen, FNAC of nodes, sputum; HIV test, blood sugar

**Q18. How do you read a Mantoux test?**
- 0.1 ml (5 TU PPD-S or 2 TU PPD RT23) intradermally on volar forearm, read at 48–72 h as transverse diameter of induration
- ≥10 mm positive in general population; ≥5 mm in HIV/immunosuppressed; very strong (≥15 mm or vesiculation) in tuberculids/LV
- False negative: anergy, HIV, malnutrition, miliary TB, measles, steroids; false positive: BCG, NTM

**Q19. What is a therapeutic trial and when is it justified?**
- When clinical suspicion is strong but bacteriology and histology are inconclusive
- Full four-drug daily regimen for 5–6 weeks; definite improvement supports TB — no response should prompt re-evaluation for other causes
- Use judiciously because of drug toxicity and risk of resistance

**Q20. What is the treatment of cutaneous TB (NTEP)?**
- Same as extra-pulmonary TB — daily fixed-dose combination by weight band
- Intensive phase 2 months: isoniazid + rifampicin + pyrazinamide + ethambutol (HRZE); continuation phase 4 months: HRE (isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol) — total 6 months; may be extended (e.g. to 9–12 months) by the clinician for slow response or associated bone/CNS disease
- Drug-resistant TB (rifampicin resistance on CBNAAT): refer for NTEP DR-TB regimens (e.g. BPaLM — bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid, moxifloxacin — 6 months)
- Pyridoxine with INH; check LFT; Nikshay registration and Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana nutrition support; surgical excision for small LV, plastic repair later

**Q21. Major side effects of first-line ATT?**
- Isoniazid: hepatitis, peripheral neuropathy (prevent with pyridoxine), pellagra, lupus-like syndrome, acneiform rash
- Rifampicin: hepatitis, orange discolouration of secretions, flu-like illness, thrombocytopenia, drug interactions
- Pyrazinamide: hepatotoxicity, hyperuricaemia/gout, photosensitivity
- Ethambutol: optic neuritis (red–green colour vision), hypersensitivity
- Cutaneous drug reactions: commonest culprit — first-line drugs cause maculopapular rash, DRESS, SJS/TEN, lichenoid eruption, FDE

**Q22. How do you assess response to treatment?**
- Clinical: lesions flatten and stop spreading in 4–6 weeks; ulcers heal; sinus discharge stops
- Most heal by the end of 6 months; residual scarring is common

**Q23. What is BCG-related skin disease?**
- Normal: papule → ulcer → scar in 6–12 weeks
- Complications: local abscess, regional lymphadenitis (suppurative), lupus vulgaris at site, keloid, disseminated BCG-osis in immunodeficiency (SCID, HIV)
- BCG reactivation at injection site in Kawasaki disease

**Q24. What is the difference between atypical mycobacterial infection and TB of skin?**
- NTM (M. marinum — fish-tank granuloma, sporotrichoid nodules on hand; M. ulcerans — Buruli ulcer; M. fortuitum/chelonae/abscessus — post-procedure abscesses after injections, liposuction, pedicure)
- NTM: from environment, not person-to-person; often resistant to standard ATT — needs clarithromycin, doxycycline, rifampicin/ethambutol, amikacin by species

**Q25. Histopathology of lupus vulgaris?**
- Tuberculoid granulomas (epithelioid cells, Langhans giant cells, lymphocytes) in upper and mid dermis, usually with little or no caseation
- Epidermis may be atrophic, ulcerated or hyperplastic; AFB rarely seen

**Q26. Why is scrofuloderma classed as multibacillary but tuberculids as having no bacilli?**
- Scrofuloderma: direct spread from a bacilli-rich deep focus with intermediate immunity
- Tuberculids: strong immunity clears organisms, leaving immune-mediated inflammation (antigen/DNA may be detected by PCR)

**Q27. How do you differentiate lupus vulgaris from sarcoidosis clinically and on histology?**
- Clinical: LV is unilateral, slowly spreading, with scarring and ulceration; sarcoid is often symmetrical, non-ulcerating, with systemic features
- Histology: LV has tuberculoid granulomas with dense lymphocytes, sometimes caseation; sarcoid has 'naked' granulomas with sparse lymphocytes, no caseation
- Mantoux: LV strongly positive; sarcoid often negative (anergy)

**Q28. Prognosis?**
- Excellent with full ATT; complications only from delay — scarring, deformities, SCC in long-standing lupus vulgaris

**Q29. What is the role of IGRA versus Mantoux in skin TB?**
- IGRA (QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus, T-SPOT.TB) measures IFN-γ release to ESAT-6/CFP-10 — not affected by BCG or most NTM, single visit, but cannot distinguish latent vs active and costly; both support diagnosis in paucibacillary forms and tuberculids when combined with clinical and histological evidence

**Q30. What are the newer Indian molecular diagnostics?**
- CBNAAT/GeneXpert MTB/RIF and Xpert Ultra, TrueNat MTB/RIF (Indian chip-based, battery-operated) — rapid detection with rifampicin resistance; Line Probe Assay (first- and second-line drugs: INH, FQ, aminoglycosides); MGIT liquid culture for DST — recommended by NTEP for extrapulmonary samples

**Q31. What is TB-HIV coinfection's effect on skin TB?**
- More multibacillary forms (miliary, gummas, orificial, scrofuloderma), atypical lesions, negative tuberculin, IRIS after ART (paradoxical worsening); give ATT first, start ART within 2–8 weeks depending on CD4; cotrimoxazole prophylaxis

## Quick spotter facts
- Apple-jelly nodules on diascopy — lupus vulgaris (also sarcoid)
- Sinus + undermined ulcer + bridge scars over neck nodes — scrofuloderma
- Warty plaque on the knee of barefoot worker — TBVC

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e ch. 16 (Cutaneous tuberculosis); NTEP (India) treatment guidance. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
